Chapter 1: Questioning Inherited Power and the Roots of Political Authority
Let’s kick off our journey into the foundations of government by really questioning something that used to seem obvious: the idea that rulers deserve their power just because of who their parents were.
For centuries, people all over the world just sort of accepted that kings and queens ruled by divine right, or as if their authority was just a natural extension of parental power.
Think about that analogy for a second—the king is the father, the people are his children, and everyone’s supposed to obey, simply because that’s the way things are.
But, does that comparison really hold up?
Parental authority isn’t meant to last forever, right? As kids grow up, they become independent, make their own choices, and start their own families.
A parent’s authority is based on care and guidance—not some endless right to control. So, when we try to stretch that model to justify a king’s lifelong, unchecked rule, it just doesn’t fit. Adults aren’t children forever, and nobody’s meant to be ruled forever, either.
There’s another problem, too. The belief that the right to rule can be inherited, like a family heirloom, brings up a whole mess of practical and moral questions.
If every ruler’s claim to power has to be traced back to a single ancestor—let’s say, the biblical Adam—how could anyone possibly prove they’re the rightful ruler, after centuries of tangled family trees? It’s just not realistic, and the whole idea of a divine or natural right starts to fall apart.
All of this leads us to a much deeper question: If inherited authority can’t be the foundation for government, then where does real political power actually come from?
The answer isn’t in bloodlines or old traditions. It’s in people themselves—and the agreements they make with each other.
So, to look for a more just and reasonable basis for government, we need to start with the state of nature. Imagine a world before any government existed. In this state, everyone’s free and equal, not subject to anyone else’s will. Each person can make their own choices, chase their own dreams, and look after their own safety. There’s no king by default—authority doesn’t just appear out of thin air, or from someone’s family tree.
Instead, real political power is born from the natural rights and mutual agreements that people create together.
This way of thinking is a real turning point. Instead of just accepting inherited power as something that’s bound to happen, we start to ask: What makes a government truly legitimate? What principles should shape the way we build our communities?
These are the questions at the heart of our exploration, guiding us as we move from challenging absolute monarchy to building a new, fairer framework for civil society.
